rv.q: The show's one saving grace is its heart, which beats strong and true throughout this homespun tale of a prodigal son who returns to his blue-collar New Jersey hometown to save his mother's house from foreclosure.

And given the musical's two-or-three year gestation period, director Rando had plenty of time to trim the repetitions (and cut a couple gratuitous stereotypes from the secondary character line-up). Every bar band has to learn when its riffs are wearing thin.
The arc of both its primary storyline and its many subplots are so grindingly predictable that the whole show might have been assembled by a pop culture algorithm tuned to maximize sentimentality.
The same could be said of this show.
Groans and cliches come fast and furious in this cheesy musical.
In so widely navigating around any real issue, its escapism starts to feel a little craven.
It is at once so bad and so bland that it erases itself even as you are watching it.
The show aims so low that all it achieves is a ruckus in the tuchis.
A community-theater vanity production that has somehow surfaced at a Broadway house, it is schlocky at every turn.
Gettin’ the Band Back Together is a warm, infectious delight.

This is a highly entertaining show with a terrific cast, supported by a bright and colorful cartoon-looking set design by Derek McLane, great costumes (especially for the character of Tygen Billows and his band members) by Emily Rebholz, and the actual band conducted by Sonny Paladino.
Regardless of the show’s inanity, I was almost embarrassed to be enjoying it as much as I was.

From its first moments, Gettin’ The Band Back Together feels like the tackiest show on Broadway, an impression advanced by its lazy plot, uninspired garage rock score, dopey jokes, and clichéd characters.

To keep with the musical parlance of the title, Gettin' the Band Back Together is like hearing an artist cover a favorite song — it’s not the first time you’ve heard it, and it might not be all that original, but you’ll be smiling and tapping your feet just the same.
Whether it's large enough to fill a Broadway house for any length of time remains to be seen.
Gettin' the Band Together feels remarkably unoriginal.

However, this statement belies the fact that the show is both generic and clichéd, borrowing pieces of much more successful shows such as The Full Monty, School of Rock, Bandstand, Groundhog Day, The Wedding Singer, and going all the way back to Bye Bye Birdie.
It’s so full of Jersey namechecks—conspicuous verisimilitude amid the consumption—that one starts to suspect paid product placement, and yet its 1990s Central Jerseyans call it Six Flags.
A lot of the right components are there, but ultimately Getting the Band Back can’t escape a basic lack of purpose and emotional investment at its core.
The plot of Gettin’ the Band Back Together is sophomoric and unrealistic.
This fleeting seed of distinction is gone too soon, lost in the amiable, directionless winds of Western Eastern Central Middlesex County.
Director John Rando (“Urinetown”) brings his signature manic style to material that resists any kind of creative tampering.
An overwhelming feeling of déjà vu—or, to quote one of Mark Allen’s more insightful lyrics—“disappointment mixed with déjà vu”—underscores Gettin’ the Band Back Together.

Some very nice, talented people have gotten themselves into Getting' the Band Back Together, which can be best described as a tribute-band version of a Broadway musical -- it has the form but none of the content.
But that's really the problem with Gettin' the Band Back Together: It consistently makes you wish you were watching something else.

Near the end of the show, Mitch receives tickets to see “Springsteen on Broadway,” which has the demoralizing effect of reminding the audience that it is instead stuck seeing “Gettin’ the Band Back Together.”
It is one of the most enjoyable shows I have seen in a while!

The creative wit who oversaw “Urinetown,” “Avenger,” “Apparent” and “All in the Timing” takes a deliberately jokey rock musical by Ken Davenport and, with excellent timing and staging, pokes fun at the genre as well as the state of New Jersey.

Even if it lacks the finesse of more highbrow fare and boasts a blandly nondescript rock score that is staggeringly forgettable, it hits every beat where it should, summons a tonally complete world, and more than once left me both rolling my eyes and crying with laughter.
What gives the show some oomph despite the inherent flaws are some dynamic numbers.

"Nothing is particularly believable, and the one character who attempts an exaggerated Jersey accent sounds like she comes from Brooklyn...Despite these flaws, I was still impressed by the production’s buoyant, almost manic energy, and laughed at many of the jokes...

In terms of this rock ensemble, however, it can easily be said that lightning does strike near enough to satisfy large portions of the show’s potential audience, particularly those who appreciate a modest story about recapturing abandoned dreams.
By the time the show began, I already knew that it was going to be a long night.
If only it felt a little less old and a little more good.
This could have been a really fun night. But maybe 'Gettin' the Band Back Together,' even though it is already on Broadway, needs some serious fine tuning.
As for how you'll feel watching 'Gettin' the Band Back Together,' be prepared to grit your teeth.
Maybe this musical could succeed there, but it won’t on Broadway.
Very little of this is amusing, much is risible, and nothing’s memorable.
The show grows increasingly desperate and reactionary...The plot sinks lower and lower into audience pandering.
What is worse is when the clichés start piling up and the dialogue and setups become juvenile and dreary.
Which, come to think of it, is a fairly apt metaphor for this entire endeavor.

cn.t: Critics find this original Jersey-set rock musical aggressively formulaic and pandering, though some appreciate its self-aware goofiness and energetic cast. Most dismiss it as tacky and desperate, while a few embrace its unpretentious, crowd-pleasing charm.

vs.sum: The Belasco Theatre offers stunning ambiance with its historic Tiffany lamps and stained-glass ceiling, but suffers from tight legroom typical of older venues. While sound quality is generally good, sightlines can be inconsistent, especially from side orchestra seats.

acc.note: 8 wheelchair locations in Orchestra. Induction loops for t-coil hearing aids. Infrared devices available.
